http://www.europesun.com/news/279205966/.text: EU caves in on new Russia sanctions media RT.com 23 Jul 2026, 17:30 GMT+10 The bloc has been forced to approve a watered-down package, including a Greek-backed exemption that allows EU companies to transport Russian LNG The EU has relented on objections from member states, granting what one diplomat has described as an "outrageous exemption," to issue a watered-down sanctions package targeting Russia. Greece successfully lobbied to allow EU companies to continue transporting Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG) to third countries, media reports claimed on Thursday. The package, the EU's 21st since the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in February 2022, was presented by the European Commission in June. It was designed to target Russia's energy, financial, crypto, trade, and fisheries sectors, bar entry to former Russian servicemen, and phase out Russian LNG transportation by EU companies. The bloc held several failed rounds of talks on the package, which requires unanimous approval from all 27 EU member states, with a number of nations arguing that some of the proposals would harm their economic interests. Greece, which has the world's largest independent cross-trade LNG fleet by capacity, warned that banning EU shipping companies from transporting Russian LNG would harm Greek shipping interests, including Dynagas. Dynagas, one of the few European companies that operate ice-class LNG carriers capable of reaching Russia's Yamal LNG project in the Arctic, says its vessels are tied to contracts running until 2065 that predate the Ukraine conflict. It argued that the sanctions could force it to sell its fleet, weakening Europe's shipping industry while benefiting foreign competitors. Greece also reportedly warned that the measure could trigger widespread reflagging to jurisdictions where EU rules would be harder to enforce, and pushed for an indefinite exemption. According to Euractiv and Euronews, citing diplomats, under a compromise brokered by the EU's rotating presidency which is held by Ireland, ambassadorssigned offon the package on Thursday after agreeing to a renewable 12-month waiver allowing the Greek company and other EU companies to continue transporting Russian LNG, subject to annual reviews. They also approved a 12-month freeze on adjustments to the G7's $44.10-per-barrel price cap on Russian oil. Without the move, the cap would have automatically increased on Thursday under a mechanism linked to global oil prices, which Brussels reportedly opposed as it would have raised the ceiling to $58 per barrel, benefiting Russia. Watered-down deal Apart from the Greek concession, the final package is reportedly significantly diluted. A Baltic-backed proposal to ban Russians who served in the military after the escalation of the Ukraine conflict from entering the bloc was scaled back after France,Italy, and Greece pushed back. The measure now only applies to short-stay visas and narrows the criteria from general military service to direct participation in military operations. EU envoys also reportedly dropped plans to phase out Russian fish imports following resistance from Germany, Poland, and Portugal, which sought to protect domestic processors. Efforts to sanction Patriarch Kirill, the head of the Russian Orthodox Church, were also reportedly blocked after opposition from Bulgaria and Italy, ensuring his removal from the blacklist. The package, however, reportedly blacklists around 250 individuals and entities accused of supporting Russia's military operation against Ukraine, "spreading propaganda," or helping circumvent sanctions, as well as more than 600 vessels linked to the supposed 'shadow fleet', which allegedly helps Russia bypass sanctions on oil exports. It also targets Russian banks, crypto platforms, and oil traders. The final version of the package must still undergo technical revisions before being adopted by all 27 member states. Behind Brussels' 'united front' Analysts and diplomats say the long-debated package highlights growing divisions within the bloc as the sanctions increasingly clash with member states' economic interests. "There's no more low-hanging fruit, with 20 packages done," one EU diplomat told Politico. Some say the standoff exposes the fact that there was never actual unanimity on sanctions, and that former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orban's departure has deprived other EU capitals of a convenient shield. For years, the scapegoating of Orban allowed other governments to hide behind Budapest while defending their own economic interests. With Peter Magyar now in office and Hungary no longer blocking the sanctions, the objections have openly surfaced. "It has been a surprise and a disappointment how many member states have stalled in their actions," Finnish MEP Ville Niinisto told Politico. Another diplomat said: "Orban was difficult, but he never actually blocked whole packages." READ MORE: Orbans exit through global eyes: Who really gains and who doesnt The package comes as the EU continues to face soaring energy costs after slashing most Russian energy imports following the escalation of the Ukraine conflict, and according to consultancy Wood Mackenzie,risksentering the upcoming heating season with its lowest gas reserves in 15 years. The bloc still imports Russian LNG, which accounts for around 14% of its supplies, even as Brussels prepares to ban purchases from January 1. The EU imported a record 9.89 million tons of LNG from Russia's Yamal project in the first half of 2026, the Financial Times reported earlier this week. Moscow has long maintained that the sanctions will not alter its political course or have a decisiveimpacton its economy, while analysts have warned that the sanctions largely backfire on those that impose them. https://www.mirror.co.uk/news/world-news.text: NATO fighter jets have downed a drone over Lithuania with the country's leader stating the country will 'defend its airspace'. Lithuania's president Gitanas Nausėda wrote on X: "A drone that just entered Lithuanian airspace was destroyed by NATO fighter jets . I thank Allied personnel for their swift response. "With Russia intensifying its aggression against Ukraine , such readiness is vital for our region. Together with our NATO Allies , Lithuania will defend its airspace." Lithuania officially joined the NATO in 2004. NATO, a 32-member alliance, was formed in 1949 to counter the risk of Soviet attack. It now focusses protecting ally counties by promising that an attack on one member is considered an attack on all. Officials said the drone entered the Lithuania's airspace from neighbouring Belarus , reports LBC News - Belarus is a Russian ally. An emergency alert was sent to mobile phones in Vilnius, Trakai and Elektrėnai shortly after midnight and residents were warned of a potential aerial threat. They were also urged to seek shelter. The drone was destroyed around 30 minutes later, the country's National Crisis Management Centre said. This is first time a drone has been shot down inside Lithuanian territory. Just one day earlier, Vilnius Airport was briefly shut over a suspected drone threat that was later found to have been caused by a flock of birds. Radar signatures from birds and drones can initially appear similar, authorities said.

https://telex.hu/belfold/2026/10/01/magy.text: Menü Kereső Bocsánatkérést vár Magyar Péter a paptól, aki azt mondta, a tiszások egy olyan erkölcsileg romlott társaságra szavaztak, amelyik elpusztítja az országot Belföld Vida Benjámin Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom Az Orbán Viktorért rendszeresen miséző plébános, Osztie Zoltán erősen politikai tartalmú szentbeszédet tartott a feldebrői Szent Márton templomban szeptember 26-án. Osztie először a megbotránkozásról beszélt, majd úgy fogalmazott: „Hány olyan keresztény testvérünk van, ki templomba jár, Tiszára szavaz, nem ért semmit. Csak épp a lényegből semmit. Hogyan a lehetséges az, hogy aki magát kereszténynek mondja, az egy erkölcsileg mélységesen romlott társaságra képes voksolni, szavazni, amelyik elpusztítja az országot.” Majd azzal folytatta, hogy az ilyen ember nem ért semmit az evangéliumból. „Egy konszenzuális, szexuális kapcsolat az alternatívája, amelyre voksol, amely mellett leteszi a hitvallást, szemben azzal, hogy a házasság és a család szent.” Osztie azt mondta, sok tévelygő ember van, aki ilyen módon szembe megy az evangéliumi élettel, és voksol a hazugságra, az erkölcstelenségre, a gyűlöletre. „Nem mi gyűlölködünk. Nem mi vagyunk azok, akik megosztjuk a társadalmat vagy az egyház életét. Azok, akik szembe mennek az evangéliummal kereszténynek mondva magukat. Micsoda ellentmondás ez! Semmit nem értenek az evangéliumból? Nem. Úgy látszik, hogy semmit nem értenek. Egy hitetlen, erkölcstelen, nemzetáruló, amely kiárusítja az országot a nagyhatalmaknak, a pénzügyi köröknek. Ez kell a magyarnak? Ez kell az országnak? Nem” – fogalmazott a plébános. Osztie azt mondta, büszke arra, hogy körülötte nincsenek tiszás szavazók, és szeretné, ha mégis vannak ilyenek, akkor nem lennének. „Olyanok vannak, akik igenis a patrióta álláspontot képviselik, az evangélium szerint élnek és nem ellenségek” – tette hozzá. A plébános szerint ők nem hallgathatnak, és nem félnek, mert ha Krisztus velük, akkor ki ellenük. Osztie a beszéde végén a tudatlanságról beszélt, és azt mondta, „az ember ésszel él, ha normális. Ha nem normális, nem ésszel él. Tiszára szavaz.” Magyar Péter a Facebook-oldalán megosztotta a több mint 13 perces mise vonatkozó részletét, és közölte, hogy Magyarország miniszterelnökeként és magánemberként is elvárja a Katolikus Egyház „azonnali, nyilvános és teljes elhatárolódását Osztie Zoltán katolikus plébános vállalhatatlan, embertelen és a kereszténységgel mindenben szembemenő mondataitól”. A kormányfő azt írta, hogy Osztie Zoltán már többször megnyilvánult pártpolitikai kérdésekben vállalhatatlan és méltatlan módon, de a mostani alkalommal ezt egy templomban, a prédikáció keretében tette. Szerinte ez teljességgel megengedhetetlen, és szembe megy a kereszténység tanításával és az alapvető emberi jóérzéssel is. Magyar szerint a kritikával sosincs gond, de nem hiszi, hogy „akár egy hívő, akár egy ateista honfitársunknak el kellene viselnie azt, hogy egy katolikus pap egy templomban ilyen stílusban és ilyen tartalommal beszéljen róla”. A miniszterelnök azt írta, tisztában van azzal, hogy Osztie Zoltán gondolatait és szavait a Katolikus Egyház sem osztja, de elvárja, hogy az elhatárolódás most a nyilvánosság előtt is megtörténjen. Hozzátette, hogy a plébánostól is bocsánatkérést vár el. „Magyar miniszterelnökként nagyra becsülöm a magyarországi egyházak szociális, oktatási, kulturális és hitéleti tevékenységét. Pontosan tudom, hogy mennyi láthatatlan és nélkülözhetetlen feladat ellátásával segítik a honfitársainkat, de úgy vélem mind az egyházi, mind a világi életben meg kell húzni a határvonalakat” – írta Magyar. A miniszterelnök posztja végén mindenkit arra kért, hogy mellőzze az egyházellenes kommenteket és megjegyzéseket, mert Osztie szavai szerinte olyan messze állnak a kereszténységtől, mint a farizeusok Jézus tanításától. Osztie Zoltán legutóbb azzal került be a hírekbe, hogy júliusban nem a főegyházmegye engedélyével szólalt fel a Sándor-palota mellé szervezett tüntetésen, amin a résztvevők Sulyok Tamás akkori köztársasági elnök mellett és a Tisza alkotmánymódosító javaslata ellen álltak ki. Osztie akkor egyebek mellett a háttérhatalom és a BlackRock befektetési alap erejéről, a kommunista és fasiszta terror módszereiről és a Pride-ról beszélt , utóbbit szerinte „az embergyűlölet nevében” rendezte meg a Tisza. A deal between Moscow and Washington over exports of Russian diesel and fresh U.S. criticism of Ukraine's leader mark important political victories for the Kremlin, reversing some of the sanctions for its full-scale invasion of its neighbor. Log in here » A deal between Moscow and Washington over exports of Russian diesel and fresh U.S. criticism of Ukraine’s leader mark important political victories for the Kremlin, reversing some of the sanctions for its full-scale invasion of its neighbor. While the size of Russia’s diesel exports is relatively small and unlikely to significantly impact prices, the revenue will help Moscow replenish its war coffers and — more importantly — undermine efforts by Kyiv and its European allies to put up a united front against President Vladimir Putin. Along with President Donald Trump suggesting that Ukraine should get a new leader to replace President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, the developments strengthen the Kremlin’s hand at a critical junction of the war, amid relentless attacks by Russia on energy systems and other vital infrastructure. President Donald Trump and Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy shake hands while meeting during the United Nations General Assembly, Tuesday, Sept. 22, 2026, at the UN headquarters. (AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson) Ahead of next month’s midterm elections, Trump blamed a spike in diesel prices on Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries, even though the U.S.-led war in Iran has sent global energy prices soaring. Mark Galeotti, a Russia expert who heads the Mayak Intelligence consultancy, described the deal that Trump announced Friday as an “astonishing birthday present” for Putin, two days after he turned 74. While Russia’s diesel exports could be a “drop in the ocean compared with actual overall demand,” Galeotti said it was “a gift for Putin, even if a single barrel of diesel is not exported.” That’s because “it drives another and increasingly thick wedge between Trump and Zelenskyy,” he said in a podcast Sunday. Russian strikes continue despite Trump’s ‘energy truce’ Even though Trump declared Sunday that Moscow and Kyiv had agreed to an “energy truce” effective immediately, Russia continued attacking Ukraine’s energy facilities, said Zelenskyy, who has criticized the diesel deal as a show of weakness. Zelenskyy emphasized that he is open to an energy ceasefire if it includes a halt to Russian attacks on Ukraine’s power grid. Russia has not said whether it agrees to such a ceasefire, and Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Monday only that “contacts are ongoing.” Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov shrugged off Zelenskyy’s comments as an attempt “to promote his interest in a ceasefire.” “I don’t think he deserves a respite,” Lavrov said. Galeotti predicted that Putin is unlikely to halt attacks on Ukraine’s energy facilities, which he sees as “absolutely central to his winter air war strategy.” Russia stepped up aerial attacks on Ukraine in recent months with ballistic missiles and new jet-powered drones, taking advantage of Kyiv’s shortage of U.S.-made Patriot interceptors whose stockpiles have been drained by the war in Iran. Putin has repeatedly emphasized that Moscow wants a comprehensive, long-term agreement, not a temporary halt to hostilities. Asked to comment on Zelenskyy’s statement that Ukraine needs a minimum of 60 days to prepare elections, Peskov said Putin could order a ceasefire only on the day of voting. Russia’s fuel crisis causes doubts about export capacity In recent months, Ukraine launched successful aerial attacks that knocked out over half of Russia’s oil refining capacity, according to the Ukrainian Defense Ministry. The strikes caused a severe fuel crisis with long lines at gas stations, bringing the war home to millions. Ukraine also methodically struck oil terminals at the Russian Black Sea port of Novorossiysk and targeted dozens of tankers at sea, seeking to derail Moscow’s oil exports and drain Moscow’s revenues. Putin acknowledged the damage but noted that Moscow is capable of inflicting much bigger blows to Ukraine. Some officials and analysts questioned whether Russia will be able to provide diesel supplies under the deal announced by Trump. Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski voiced doubts about it, saying that even the Russian capital is experiencing fuel shortages. Others say Moscow actually has a surplus of diesel, now that demand has eased following the end of the harvest season. “Russia planned to export more diesel anyway,” said Janis Kluge, head of the Eastern Europe and Eurasia Division at the German Institute for International and Security Affairs. Still, some Russian motorists exhausted by months of waiting at gas stations were worried the new deal could leave fewer supplies for the domestic market. “I don’t think that’s very good, because you can see what’s going on at gas stations — people are standing in line around the clock,” said Marat Salavatov, waiting to refuel at a Moscow gas station. Russian officials sought to quell such fears, saying there will be enough supply to keep the domestic market stable. The volume of production is able “to fully satisfy the needs of the local market while delivering the agreed amounts to the global market,” Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said in a government statement announcing the lifting of the diesel export ban that had been in place since July. Trump’s criticism of Zelenskyy is seen as aiding Russia In addition to the diesel deal, Trump unleashed biting criticism of Zelenskyy that marks perhaps the lowest point in their relationship since the disastrous Oval Office meeting in February 2025. That could be even more important for the Kremlin. Trump’s remark that it was time for a new president in Ukraine and his suggestion that Zelenskyy has not done enough to end the war topped the news on Russian state television and was widely discussed by pro-Kremlin commentators and military bloggers. Officials in Kyiv viewed the diesel deal and the hostile rhetoric as a political move aimed at making Zelenskyy a scapegoat for U.S. voters ahead of the midterms, said Oleksandr Merezhko, a lawmaker from Zelenskyy’s party. “We are not happy when our ally and partner gives money to a dictator who is killing us,” Merezhko said. “By demanding that Ukraine stop striking Russian oil refineries, Trump looks as though he cares more about the Russian war machine than about the civilians Putin is killing.” Kyiv fears that easing sanctions without meaningful concessions from Russia could weaken Washington’s leverage over the Kremlin and further diminish prospects for fair terms to end the war. The Trump-Zelenskyy tensions come as Kyiv continues to rely heavily on Washington for military assistance, including Patriot systems and vital intelligence. A disruption of that support could leave Ukraine more vulnerable. Galeotti said Trump’s comments casting Zelenskyy as an obstacle to peace were “benefit No. 1 for Putin.” Trump’s move also raises questions about the European Union’s efforts to go after Russia’s so-called shadow fleet of tankers carrying oil to global markets, he said, observing that Europe has been left in a position “where it’s obviously just regarded as a vassal region that has to accept whatever policy comes from the White House.” The diesel deal also will boost Russia’s credentials with developing countries, helping its posture as a great global player worthy of being a partner, Galeotti said. Tatiana Stanovaya of the Carnegie Russia and Eurasia Center said the move could look like a “moment of triumph” for Putin. “He has secured an economic deal, albeit a modest one, before a peace settlement, departing from Washington’s previous position,” Stanovaya said in a commentary.
